newsitem.title: USA: Assisted suicide debate seen raging at state level.
newsitem.headline: Assisted suicide debate seen raging at state level.

text.p: The Supreme Court's refusal to grant Americans a constitutional right to assisted suicide drew cheers from physicians Thursday and a vow from Dr. Jack Kevorkian to keep working to end his patients' suffering.

The landmark decision did little to end the raging, emotional debate over doctor assisted suicide, but put control over it into the hands of state legislatures. Experts predicted that some states will eventually allow the practice and become suicide meccas.
President Clinton applauded the decision, saying assisted suicide "is wrong."
"This decision is a victory for all Americans -- it prevents us from going down a very dangerous and troubling path on this difficult and often agonizing issue," Clinton said in a statement.
Kevorkian, the wiry, 69-year-old retired pathologist who attended some 45 suicides since 1990, will continue his controversial crusade, said his lawyer Geoffrey Fieger.
"Dr. Kevorkian is not the least bit intimidated by this," Fieger told a news conference Thursday. Asked if Kevorkian will immediately resume attending suicides, Fieger said, "You never know."

Fieger called the decision an "act of hypocrisy" said it would force people to suffer needlessly and turn to violent forms of suicide, such as that chosen by actor Brian Keith, who was suffering from cancer and shot himself Tuesday.

Kevorkian, who gained a reprieve from his fourth assisted suicide trial two weeks ago when a judge declared a mistrial, was not directly involved in the New York and Washington cases that led to the Supreme Court's unanimous decision.

In Chicago, the court's ruling was greeted by cheers and shouts of approval when it was announced to the American Medical Association's House of Delegates, the annual policy meeting for the nation's largest medical group.
The AMA has strongly opposed physician-assisted suicide, saying it violates a doctor's ethical duty to heal.

"To suggest a constitutional right to physician-assisted suicide would have so fundamentally altered the relationship between the patient and his or her physician that it would have undermined the principles of medical elthics that we as a profession work to protect," said Nancy Dickey, the AMA's president-elect.
Some AMA doctors said they hope the decision will spur new efforts to improve medical care for the terminally ill.
But the physician who challenged the New York assisted suicide ban, Timothy Quill, said doctors still need laws that help them respond to difficult cases.
"How do we respond when good palliative care stops working?," Quill said. "Those kinds of solutions are still going to be done in secret, behind closed doors."
Anti-abortion groups applauded the decision but vowed pressure against assisted suicide at the state level.

"We must now mobilise in all 50 states to fight efforts to legalise direct killing of the vulnerable through state courts, state legislatures and referenda," said David O'Steen, director of the Washington-based National Right-to-Life Committee Inc.

But the court's move to give states the authority to ban assisted suicide also gave them the ability to allow assisted suicide, as Oregon did in a 1994 referendum, which has been on hold pending a second referendum in November.

In Kevorkian's home state of Michigan, public opinion polls show that more than 60 percent of residents support assisted suicide. Michigan has no statute governing the practice, although the state's supreme court has declared it illegal based on unwritten "common law."

"If I had to predict, I would predict that we will see a few states legalise this practice and we will see people travelling to those states even if they have to meet some sort of residency requirement," said Susan Wolf, a professor of law and medicine at the University of Minnesota Law School. "We will see more litigation about all this."
